domain: Measurement science and evaluation methodology — construct validity, inter-rater reliability, and LLM-as-judge design; the applied discipline behind eval-harness design, human-eval calibration studies, and Goodhart's-law-aware metric design in ML systems
axioms: Every gate or judge is a proxy for a construct it cannot directly observe; a proxy is useful only to the extent its correlation with the true construct has actually been checked, never merely assumed.

A measurement instrument can be gamed by any actor scored by it — the moment a metric becomes a target, the optimizing pressure on the metric diverges from the optimizing pressure on the construct unless the two are provably identical (Goodhart's law).

Two measurements of 'the same thing' by the same method against the same input are not independent evidence — re-running an identical procedure on an identical input measures the procedure's own variance (reliability), not the underlying truth (validity).

A judge's criteria can only be as complete as the domain expertise that authored them; criteria authored by the same party whose work they will later evaluate carry a conflict-of-interest risk on completeness, independent of anyone's good faith.

Self-report is a low-validity channel by default; it requires either independent verification or a structural reason the reporter cannot benefit from misreporting before it can be trusted as ground truth.

An evaluation result is interpretable only relative to the population and conditions it was measured under; results from a small or non-representative pilot generalize only as far as that pilot's own structure allows.
A verdict format that admits no partial or ambiguous state (pure PASS/FAIL) forces every edge case into the examiner's undocumented discretion, which quietly becomes a second, unaudited criterion.
primitives: construct (the actual property the design needs measured, e.g. 'main-thread context bloat')
proxy metric (the token-share gate, standing in for the construct)
judge / rater (the validator, and what it does or does not share with the executor's own check)
criteria / rubric (the plan's frozen criteria — authored by the same party that will be judged against them)
reliability vs. validity (does a repeated measurement agree with itself, versus does it agree with the truth)
self-report (the executor's verbatim verify output, taken on trust)
sample / pilot (the three planned pilot runs, and what they can and cannot generalize to)
failure_mode: Focuses on whether an instrument measures the right thing, so it can miss failures that are purely mechanical — a message lost, a lock not taken — even when those mechanical failures would also corrupt the measurement; it will diagnose 'wrong construct' when the real bug is 'the input pipeline drops data', which looks identical from this lens.

Assumes rational, if imperfectly informed, actors constructing and gaming metrics in the abstract; it has no native vocabulary for why one specific actor — as opposed to metrics in general — is incentivized toward a particular defection, which is principal-agent territory, not measurement science.

Tends to demand more rigorous validation (calibration studies, inter-rater agreement measurement) than a fast-moving three-pilot phase can afford, and can under-weight that a somewhat-invalid gauge deployed now with a plan to recalibrate is sometimes the right call against the alternative of shipping with no gauge at all.

Treats each gate or verdict as a standalone instrument to be validated on its own terms, and is weak at reasoning about how instruments compose — e.g. whether a valid executor self-report combined with a redundant validator check produces a system that is jointly less reliable than either part alone.
